chapter.title: Nietzsche and the modern turn: who decides what is true or good

cards.body: *God is dead* sounds like a boast, but when Nietzsche wrote it in 1882 it worked more like a smoke alarm. At our long dinner table, the guests have argued for over 2,000 years about which rules are right. Nietzsche stands up, lifts the tablecloth and asks **who set this table, and who got the best seats?**
cards.simpler: When Nietzsche wrote *God is dead* in 1882, he wasn't bragging. He was sounding a warning, like a smoke alarm. Picture a long dinner table where people have argued for over 2,000 years about which rules are right. Nietzsche stands up, lifts the tablecloth, and asks **who set this table, and who got the best seats?**

cards.prompt: Nietzsche has just lifted the tablecloth. If *God is dead* is a warning, what is it warning about?

options.text: Religion makes people unhappy, so it should be banned.
If the old foundation for our values is gone, something still has to hold them up.
Plato was right, and perfect forms are the only safe ground left.

whyNot.a: That's a boast, not a warning: he wasn't cheering a win or calling for bans. He was worried about what comes next.
whyNot.c: That's chapter 3's argument, not this one: Nietzsche was suspicious of perfect forms sitting behind the world.

cards.reteach: For centuries, many Europeans rested right and wrong on God. Nietzsche saw that belief fading and asked: if that floor goes, what keeps our values standing? The line is a question about the floor, not a victory lap.

cards.title: Values have a family tree
cards.body:
Nietzsche's big move was to treat values like old furniture: **every value was made by someone, at some time, for some reason.** Take humility. It didn't fall from the sky. People built it.

He called this kind of digging a *genealogy*, which means tracing a family tree, here for an idea instead of a person. In 1887 he wrote a whole book doing it for morality.

You'd think finding out where a value came from would settle whether it's good. It doesn't. Learning your grandmother's chair was built in a shed tells you nothing about whether it holds your weight. But it does make you check the legs.
cards.simpler: Nietzsche saw values like old furniture: **every value was made by someone, at some time, for some reason.** Humility didn't fall from the sky. People built it. He called tracing this a *genealogy*, a family tree for an idea. In 1887 he wrote a whole book on morality this way. Knowing where a value came from doesn't settle if it's good. A chair built in a shed may still hold you. But you'd check the legs.

cards.title: Phones at Sunday lunch
cards.body: Uncle Dev says phones at the table are rude, and his niece Maya, 19, replies *that's just your opinion* while reaching for the gravy. She's echoing Protagoras, a Greek teacher from the 400s BC, known for the idea that each person is the measure of what's true for them. Plato pushed back hard: if every view is true, then so is the view that Protagoras is wrong. Nietzsche would ask what neither of them did: **who made the phone rule, and whom does it serve?** That question has an actual answer, which is more than *just your opinion* can say.
cards.simpler: Uncle Dev says phones at the table are rude. His niece Maya, 19, says *that's just your opinion*, reaching for the gravy. She's echoing Protagoras, a Greek teacher from the 400s BC, who said each person decides what's true for them. Plato pushed back: if every view is true, so is the view that Protagoras is wrong. Nietzsche would ask something new: **who made the phone rule, and whom does it serve?** That question has a real answer.

cards.prompt: A coworker shrugs: 'Being on time is just a rule bosses invented.' Which reply makes the Nietzsche move?

options.text: Then it means nothing, so nobody has to bother.
Maybe. Who started it, when, and who gains from it? Then we can judge if it's worth keeping.
No, punctuality is a perfect form that exists outside time.

whyNot.a: That's the slide Nietzsche feared, not his method: a value having a maker doesn't make it worthless.
whyNot.c: That's Plato's kind of answer, not Nietzsche's: he doubted that values sit outside history.

cards.reteach: Nietzsche's move has two steps. First, trace a value back to the people who made it and why. Second, judge it with that history in view. Skip step two and you end up shrugging at everything.

cards.title: From good to true
cards.body:
Nietzsche pushed the same question past right and wrong to truth itself. He suggested that what a group calls *true* often lines up suspiciously well with what helps that group. Picture a school history book written by the side that won the war.

This is where today's arguments live. When people fight over who writes the textbook, who decides what counts as misinformation, or who gets to define *normal*, they're sitting in his chair.

Now the reversal: **Nietzsche didn't conclude that nothing matters.** He thought that conclusion was the real disaster coming. He wanted people brave enough to make values worth living by.
cards.simpler: Nietzsche took the same question past right and wrong to truth itself. He noticed that what a group calls *true* often fits neatly with what helps that group, like a history book written by the side that won the war. Today's fights over who writes textbooks or who decides what's *normal* come from here. But **Nietzsche didn't conclude that nothing matters.** He saw that as the coming disaster. He wanted people brave enough to make values worth living by.

cards.body: Sam reads one Nietzsche line on a poster, decides all values are invented, and announces that the flat's washing-up rota is now *just a social construct*. Three days later the sink smells like a pond. Sam took *made by people* to mean *not worth keeping*, which is exactly the slide Nietzsche warned about. Spot it whenever someone uses a value's history as a reason to stop thinking instead of a reason to start.
cards.simpler: Sam reads one Nietzsche line on a poster and decides all values are made up. So the flat's washing-up rota is now *just a social construct*, meaning something people invented. Three days later the sink smells like a pond. Sam took *made by people* to mean *not worth keeping*, the exact slide Nietzsche warned about. **Watch for anyone using a value's history as a reason to stop thinking**, when it should be a reason to start.

cards.prompt: Three guests at the long table. Which sentence is Nietzsche's?

options.text: Every opinion is equally true for the person who holds it.
Values were made by people, so ask who made them and why, then decide which are worth keeping.
Right and wrong are fixed and timeless, waiting to be discovered.

whyNot.a: That's Protagoras, not Nietzsche: Nietzsche asks where a value came from, not whether all views tie.
whyNot.c: That's closer to Plato's side, not Nietzsche's: he treated values as having a history.

cards.reteach: Think of three guests at dinner. Protagoras says every dish is good to whoever likes it. Plato says there's one perfect recipe out there. Nietzsche asks who cooked each dish and for whom, then tastes it anyway.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
Nietzsche argued that our values have a history: people made them, at certain times, often to suit themselves. That doesn't make them worthless; it means **you can ask who made a value and why before deciding to keep it.**

Next: Wittgenstein's idea that many of these puzzles come from how we use words.
cards.simpler: Nietzsche argued that our values have a history. People made them, at certain times, often to suit themselves. That doesn't make them worthless. It means **you can ask who made a value and why before deciding to keep it.** Next up is Wittgenstein, who thought many of these puzzles come from the way we use words.

cards.body: Tonight, pick one house rule you follow without thinking, like shoes off at the door. Ask three things: who started it, when, and who it helps. Then decide: keep it, change it, or drop it.
cards.simpler: Tonight, pick one house rule you follow without thinking, like taking your shoes off at the door. Ask three things: who started it, when, and who it helps. Then, with those answers in hand, **decide whether to keep it, change it, or drop it.**

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now hear 'that's just your opinion', link it to Protagoras, name Plato as the one who pushed back, and ask Nietzsche's question: who made this value, and why?
